chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Hakim, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The absentee's debts are paid from him when evidence is established against him, and his property is sold while he is absent, and the absentee remains upon his proof when he arrives, and the money is not handed over to the one who established the evidence except with a guarantor, if he is not wealthy.

key_terms.الْبَيِّنَةُ: The evidence; proof presented by the creditor to establish the debt.
key_terms.الْغَائِبُ: The absentee; a person who is away and whose whereabouts are unknown or who is delaying payment.
key_terms.بِكُفَلَاءَ: With a guarantor; requiring a surety to ensure the creditor receives the funds or to secure the transaction.
key_terms.حُجَّتِهِ: His proof; the right of the absentee to present his case or evidence upon returning.
key_terms.مَلِيّاً: Wealthy; possessing sufficient means, implying a creditor with wealth might not need a guarantor.
key_terms.يُقْضَى عَنْهُ: Paid from him; referring to the settlement of debts using the absentee's assets.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on settling the debts of an absent person whose property is being sold?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the jurisprudential principle that an absentee's (gha'ib) property can be liquidated to settle verified debts, reflecting the Shia emphasis on balancing creditor rights with the debtor's protection against fraud. The requirement of a guarantor (kafala) for releasing funds, unless the creditor is wealthy (mali), underscores the scholarly concern for financial security in the absence of the debtor. This mechanism ensures that the absentee retains his 'hujjah' (right to claim) upon return, preserving the integrity of the transaction within the broader framework of Islamic commercial law.
